title: Basic types and explicit conversion
summary: Go never converts between numeric types for you, not even int to int64. Every conversion is visible, and named types like Celsius carry meaning the compiler enforces.

examples.title: Mixing numeric types needs a conversion, and conversions have rules

annotations.note: int and int64 are distinct types even where int is 64 bits wide. The commented line is a compile error; the conversion makes the widening visible at the exact spot it happens.
The same for float64 and int. Untyped constants are the exception: price * 3 compiles, because the literal 3 takes on float64.
Float to int truncates toward zero: -2.9 becomes -2, not -3. Use math.Floor or math.Round first when you mean those.
Narrowing a variable keeps the low bits: 200 fits uint8 but reads as -56 in int8. With a constant, int8(200) is a compile error instead.
Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^32 here. Nothing panics on integer overflow in Go, signed or unsigned.
Integer division truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the dividend: -3 and -1. Python floors instead and gives -4 and 1.
Celsius and Fahrenheit share float64 underneath, so converting between them is allowed, but only when written out. Assigning one to the other is the bug the type exists to catch.
time.Duration is a named int64 counting nanoseconds. An int variable must be converted before multiplying, and a bare 2 is two nanoseconds.
strconv.Itoa formats digits; string(rune(65)) is the code point "A". Writing string(n) for an int n is the classic mix-up, and go vet flags it.
Parsing returns the zero value plus an error that names the function and the input: no exception, no NaN.
strconv follows Go syntax, not a locale. A Turkish decimal comma ("3,14") is a syntax error, so normalize user input at the boundary.

use_cases: Converting between int sizes at API boundaries (database int64 ids, len() int results)
Named types for units and identifiers: type UserID int64, type Celsius float64
time.Duration arithmetic for timeouts and backoff
strconv for parsing and formatting numbers from flags, query strings and CSV
strengths: No implicit conversions means no silent truncation or sign changes hidden in arithmetic, unlike C's usual arithmetic conversions
Named types give unit and ID safety for free: passing a UserID where an OrderID is expected doesn't compile, unlike TypeScript's structural number aliases
Parsing errors are values that say what failed and on which input
weaknesses: Conversions add noise in numeric code, e.g. float64(len(xs)) in every average
Integer overflow wraps silently at run time; there is no checked arithmetic as in Rust's debug builds
Named types over the same base convert freely when written out, so a careless Fahrenheit(c) still compiles

pitfalls.title: string(n) on an integer
pitfalls.detail: It produces the character with that code point, not decimal digits. Use strconv.Itoa or fmt.Sprint.

pitfalls.title: Expecting float-to-int to round
pitfalls.detail: int(f) truncates toward zero. Round explicitly with math.Round when you need it.

pitfalls.title: Narrowing without a range check
pitfalls.detail: int32(x) on an out-of-range int64 keeps the low bits and changes the value. Check the range first when the input isn't under your control.

quiz.q: var a int = 1; var b int64 = 2. Does a + b compile?
options: Yes, int is 64 bits on amd64
No: mismatched types int and int64
quiz.why: Distinct types never mix in arithmetic, whatever their size on the platform.
The fraction is discarded: truncation toward zero.
Duration counts nanoseconds; write 5 * time.Second for seconds.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Conversions
The Go Programming Language Specification: Arithmetic operators

body:
## Concept

Go's basic types are `bool`, `string`, sized integers (`int8`…`int64`, `uint8`…`uint64`,
plus `int`/`uint` at the platform's word size), `float32`/`float64`, and aliases `byte`
(`uint8`) and `rune` (`int32`). Values of different types never mix: you write the
conversion `T(x)` yourself. A *named type* such as `type Celsius float64` is a new type
with the same underlying representation; it converts to and from `float64` explicitly,
never implicitly.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: no integer promotion and no usual arithmetic conversions. `int + int64` is a
  compile error, so a sign or width change always shows up as a conversion in the code.
- Java widens `int` to `long` automatically; Go doesn't widen at all. There is no
  boxing either: no `Integer` objects.
- Python: Go integers have a fixed size and wrap on overflow, and integer `/` and `%`
  truncate toward zero where Python's `//` and `%` floor.
- JS/TS: no single `number` type. TS `type UserId = number` is only an alias, while Go's
  `type UserID int64` is a distinct type the compiler checks.

## Design notes

Convert at the boundary and keep one type inside: parse strings with `strconv` where
input enters, convert database `int64` ids once in the store layer, and let named types
(`UserID`, `Celsius`, `time.Duration`) carry meaning through the rest of the code. When
a conversion narrows a value you don't control, check the range first: Go wraps silently
on overflow. For user-facing numbers in Turkish (decimal comma, dot as thousands
separator), normalize the text before `strconv.ParseFloat`, which only accepts Go syntax.

files.examples/01_explicit.go:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var count int = 3
	var total int64 = 10
	// fmt.Println(count + total) // compile error: mismatched types int and int64
	fmt.Println(int64(count) + total)

	price := 9.99
	// fmt.Println(price * count) // compile error: mismatched types float64 and int
	fmt.Printf("%.2f\n", price*float64(count))

	f := -2.9
	fmt.Println(int(f), int(-f)) // truncates toward zero: not floor, not round

	n := 200
	fmt.Println(uint8(n), int8(n)) // same 8 bits, different meaning: 200 vs -56

	var u uint32
	u-- // unsigned arithmetic wraps around instead of failing
	fmt.Println(u)

	a, b := -7, 2
	fmt.Println(a/b, a%b) // integer division truncates toward zero too
}
